passage: Nora checked the station clock for the fifth time and smiled. In ten minutes, the train from the coast would arrive, bringing her grandfather for his first visit in three years. She had spent the whole week planning every detail: the café by the river where they would have lunch, the new bookstore she wanted to show him, and the chess set she had bought so they could play again as they used to on long summer evenings. She held a small sign she had painted that morning, decorated with his favorite sunflowers, and imagined the look on his face when he saw it. Then her phone buzzed. It was a message from her mother. Her grandfather had caught a bad cold the night before, and his doctor had advised him not to travel for at least two weeks. Nora read the message twice, hoping she had misunderstood. Slowly she lowered the sign, watched the train pull in without him, and turned toward the exit, the painted sunflowers suddenly looking pale in the gray afternoon light.

passage: The pangolin is a small mammal found in parts of Africa and Asia, and it is the only mammal whose body is covered almost entirely in large, overlapping scales. These scales are made of keratin, the same material that forms human fingernails, and they protect the animal like a suit of armor. When threatened, a pangolin rolls itself into a tight ball that most predators find very difficult to open. Pangolins have no teeth. Instead, they use their powerful front claws to break into ant and termite nests, and then they collect the insects with a long, sticky tongue that can reach about forty centimeters in the largest species. Because they are active mainly at night and spend the day in burrows or hollow trees, they are rarely seen in the wild. Sadly, pangolins are among the most illegally traded mammals in the world, hunted both for their meat and for their scales, which are wrongly believed to have medical value. International trade in all pangolin species has been banned since 2017, but protecting them remains a major challenge.
question: pangolin에 관한 다음 글의 내용과 일치하지 않는 것은?

explain_ko: 'Pangolins have no teeth'이고 앞발톱으로 개미집을 부순다고 했으므로 '이빨로 부순다'는 불일치. 케라틴 비늘, 야행성, 2017년 거래 금지는 모두 본문과 일치.

passage: Young people today can find an answer to almost any question within seconds, yet the speed of searching has not made them better at judging what they find. Surveys repeatedly show that many students trust a website simply because it appears near the top of a search results page or because it looks professionally designed. Some cannot tell the difference between a news article and an advertisement written to look like one. Warning students to be careful online is not enough, because vague warnings do not give them any practical tools. Instead, schools should teach concrete habits of checking information as a regular part of every subject. Students should learn to ask who created a source, what that person or organization might gain from it, and whether other independent sources report the same facts. A science class can examine a health claim that is spreading on social media, and a history class can compare how different websites describe the same event. Only through repeated practice will careful checking become as automatic as searching itself.

passage: Many people start the new year with ambitious exercise plans, such as running ten kilometers three times a week or spending two hours at the gym every weekend. Within a month or two, most of these plans have been abandoned. The reason is rarely laziness. Demanding routines require large blocks of free time and a high level of motivation, and both are in short supply during a busy week. When a single session is missed, the whole plan starts to feel like a failure, and people give up entirely. Research on physical activity suggests a different strategy. Short, moderate sessions, even ten or fifteen minutes of brisk walking a day, provide meaningful health benefits, including lower blood pressure and improved mood. More importantly, such small routines are easy to fit into ordinary life, so they are far more likely to be repeated until they become habits. Over the course of a year, a modest routine that is actually followed will do much more for the body than an impressive plan that exists only on paper.

passage: No language grows in isolation. Whenever communities meet through trade, travel, or conquest, words cross from one language to another, and English is a striking example: a large proportion of its vocabulary was borrowed from French, Latin, Norse, and many other sources. Borrowed words, however, rarely remain unchanged. They are usually reshaped to fit the sound system of the new language, so that sounds which do not exist in it are replaced by the closest familiar ones. Their meanings often shift as well. A word that referred to a whole category in its original language may come to name only one particular item in its new home, or it may take on a new tone, sounding more elegant, more technical, or more casual than before. Sometimes a borrowed word even returns to its original language with a changed meaning, surprising the speakers who first lent it. Tracing such journeys allows linguists to reconstruct the history of contact between peoples who left few other records.

passage: Before the nineteenth century, every town set its clocks by the sun. When the sun reached its highest point in the sky, it was noon, and because this moment arrives a little later as one moves west, the clocks of two nearby towns might differ by several minutes. For centuries this caused no real problems, since few people traveled fast enough to notice. The arrival of the railway changed everything. A train leaving one city at a certain time might arrive in another city whose clocks followed a completely different local time, and printed timetables became confusing lists of conflicting hours. More seriously, when two trains shared a single track, a misunderstanding about the time could lead to a deadly collision. To solve this problem, railway companies began to adopt a single standard time across their entire networks. Governments later followed their example, dividing countries and eventually the whole world into time zones. The hours we check on our phones today are, in a sense, a legacy of the steam engine.

passage: For most of the twentieth century, traffic engineers believed that the safest streets were those that separated cars and people as clearly as possible, with high curbs, fences, and countless signs. Some urban planners, however, have begun testing the opposite idea. ① In so-called shared spaces, curbs, traffic lights, and road markings are removed, so that drivers, cyclists, and pedestrians all use the same level surface. ② Without clear rules telling them who has priority, drivers can no longer assume that the road belongs to them, so they naturally slow down and make eye contact with the people around them. ③ Several towns that adopted this design have reported fewer serious accidents, even though their streets now look less organized than before. ④ The first electric traffic signals were installed more than a century ago, and their colors were borrowed from the signals used on railways. The lesson for planners is that safety sometimes comes not from removing uncertainty but from creating just enough of it to keep everyone alert.

passage:
To a batter, a well-thrown curveball seems to travel in a straight line and then suddenly drop or swerve at the last moment, as if it had been pulled by an invisible hand.

(A) This difference in air flow produces a difference in pressure around the ball, and the ball is pushed steadily toward the side where the pressure is lower. The same effect allows a soccer player to bend a free kick around a wall of defenders.

(B) All of this, however, happens gradually rather than suddenly. The ball bends along a smooth path the whole way to home plate, but because the batter sees it from almost directly behind, most of the sideways movement becomes noticeable only in the final few meters. The sharp break that batters describe is therefore partly a trick of perspective.

(C) The secret lies in the spin that the pitcher gives the ball on release. As the ball rotates, its raised stitches drag a thin layer of air around with it, so the air on one side of the ball moves faster than the air on the other side.

passage: Walk through the older districts of many cities and you will find entire streets lined with shops that sell almost the same things. One street is full of furniture stores, while another is crowded with lighting shops or tailors. ( ① ) Yet these shop owners are usually not making a mistake. ( ② ) For expensive goods that people buy only once in several years, such as a sofa or a wedding dress, customers want to compare styles, quality, and prices carefully before deciding. ( ③ ) A street with twenty similar stores therefore attracts far more shoppers than twenty stores scattered across the city, because visitors know they can see many options in a single trip. ( ④ ) Each shop may lose some sales to its neighbors, but it gains many more customers who would never have come to an isolated store. Clustering also brings practical benefits, as suppliers, repair workers, and delivery companies tend to set up nearby, lowering costs for everyone on the street.

passage: Many listeners in Western countries describe music in a minor key as sad and music in a major key as happy, and film composers rely on this association constantly. Because this connection feels so natural, it is easy to assume that it is built into the human brain. ( ① ) Researchers who have played Western music to people with little exposure to it, however, have found a more complicated picture. ( ② ) In several such studies, listeners from remote communities judged the emotion of songs mainly by their speed and loudness, not by whether the key was major or minor. ( ③ ) Children in Western countries, too, do not reliably link minor keys with sadness until around the age of six, although they recognize a fast tempo as cheerful much earlier. ( ④ ) Taken together, these findings suggest that the emotional meaning of a musical key is at least partly learned through years of hearing songs in films, advertisements, and celebrations, rather than simply given to us at birth.

passage: When computer programs first made it possible to record music with perfect timing, many producers were delighted. Every drumbeat could be placed exactly on the beat, and every note could be corrected to the precise pitch. Yet listeners often described the results as cold and lifeless, even when they could not explain why. Studies of skilled performers help to solve the puzzle. When human drummers play, their beats land slightly early or slightly late by a few thousandths of a second, and these tiny variations are not random. They follow patterns that respond to the other musicians and to the emotional shape of the song, pushing ahead in exciting moments and relaxing in calm ones. Listeners do not consciously notice these shifts, but they sense them as a feeling of movement and life, which musicians call groove. For this reason, many producers now deliberately add small timing variations to computer-made tracks. They have learned that perfection is not the goal of music, and that [a little imperfection is what makes the rhythm breathe].

passage: In a small village where everyone knows everyone else, people can lend tools, leave doors unlocked, and make agreements with a handshake. Such arrangements work because reputation travels quickly: anyone who cheats a neighbor will soon find that no one is willing to help them. As communities grow into cities of millions, this kind of personal monitoring becomes impossible. Most of the people we deal with each day are strangers whom we will never see again, and gossip can no longer keep everyone honest. Societies have responded by building _____ to take over the job once performed by personal relationships. Written contracts, courts, licenses, and consumer protection laws allow us to trust a taxi driver, a bank, or an online seller we have never met, because we know that dishonest behavior can be reported and punished. These systems are sometimes criticized as cold and bureaucratic, but they are precisely what makes cooperation among strangers possible on a large scale. Without them, trade and social life would shrink back to the size of a village.

passage: We usually judge a product by how well it resists breaking, but engineers often spend just as much effort deciding how it should break. Every structure will eventually fail if the load becomes large enough, and the real danger lies in failures that happen suddenly and in unexpected places. For this reason, designers deliberately build in weak points. An electrical fuse contains a thin wire that melts when the current becomes too strong, cutting the power before the wiring inside the walls can overheat and start a fire. The front section of a car is designed to crush in a collision, absorbing energy so that the passenger cabin stays in one piece. Posts that hold road signs are often attached with bolts that snap easily when a vehicle hits them, so the post falls away instead of stopping the car violently. In each case, a small, cheap part is sacrificed to protect something far more valuable. Good design, in other words, does not only aim to prevent failure; it also involves _____.

passage: Scientists interested in how wild animals acquire new skills set up feeding boxes that could be opened in two different ways. A small door on each box could either be pushed to the left or slid to the right. They trained one bird from a wild group to use the left method and another bird from a separate group to use the right method, and then returned both birds to their groups. Within a few weeks, most members of each group had learned to open the box. Nearly all of them used the same method as the trained bird in their group, even though the other method worked equally well. More surprisingly, when some birds moved from one group to the other the following year, many of them abandoned their original method and adopted the one preferred by their new neighbors. The researchers concluded that the birds were not simply solving the problem on their own. Instead, they were copying those around them, and the local habit spread and persisted much like a tradition in a human community.

W: I know what you mean. I used to have the same problem.
M: Really? How did you fix it?
W: I set a daily time limit on my apps. When the time is up, the app locks.
M: But can't you just unlock it again?
W: You can, but it makes you stop and think. Most of the time, I realize I don't really need to keep watching.
M: That sounds helpful. I have a big exam next week, and I haven't studied much yet.
W: Then this is the perfect time to start. I can help you set it up.
M: Thanks. How long do you think my daily limit should be?
question: 대화를 듣고, 남자의 마지막 말에 대한 여자의 응답으로 가장 적절한 것을 고르시오.
choices: Sure. I'll lock your phone so you can't use it.
I watched short videos for three hours, too.
Why don't you start with one hour a day?
Good luck. I hope you do well on the exam.
explain_ko: 하루 제한 시간을 얼마로 할지 물었으므로 하루 한 시간부터 해 보라는 답이 알맞음. 시험 응원은 질문(시간)에 대한 답이 아님.

passage:
M: Hi, I saw a sign saying there are garden plots available in this community garden.
W: Yes, we have a few left. Are you interested in renting one?
M: I am. I just moved into the apartment across the street, and I've always wanted to grow my own vegetables.
W: Wonderful. Each plot is two meters by three meters, and it costs forty dollars for the whole season.
M: That's reasonable. Do I need to bring my own tools?
W: No. We have shared tools in the storage shed, and there's a water tap next to every row.
M: Great. Are there any rules I should know about?
W: Just a few. You can't use chemical pesticides, and you need to visit your plot at least once a week.
M: That's fine. I plan to come almost every day.
W: Perfect. Oh, and since you're new to gardening, we hold a free workshop for beginners every Saturday morning. Would you be interested?
question: 대화를 듣고, 여자의 마지막 말에 대한 남자의 응답으로 가장 적절한 것을 고르시오.
choices: Definitely. What time does it start?
Yes. The plot costs forty dollars for the season.
Sorry, but chemical pesticides aren't allowed here.
No, I moved in about a year ago.
explain_ko: 초보자 무료 강좌에 관심 있는지 묻자 참여 의사와 시작 시간을 묻는 응답이 자연스러움. 농약 금지·가격 안내는 관리자(여자)가 한 말.

passage:
W: Uncle Tom, can I ask you something? You've sold your paintings at markets for years, right?
M: That's right. Are you thinking of selling your artwork?
W: Yes. There's a flea market at the city hall next month, and I'd like to have a booth there.
M: That's great. How many pieces do you have ready?
W: About fifteen small paintings. But I'm not sure how to set the prices.
M: For your first market, I'd keep the prices low. People are more willing to buy from new artists when the price is affordable.
W: That makes sense. What else should I prepare?
M: Bring small cards with your name and social media account. Even if people don't buy anything, they might contact you later.
W: Good idea. I never thought about that.
M: And one more thing. Some customers may want to pay by card. Do you have a way to accept card payments?
question: 대화를 듣고, 남자의 마지막 말에 대한 여자의 응답으로 가장 적절한 것을 고르시오.
choices: Yes, I have about fifteen small paintings ready.
Of course. The flea market was held last month.
Sure. I'll set high prices to look professional.
Not yet. Can you recommend a good way to do that?
explain_ko: 카드 결제 방법이 있는지 묻자 아직 없다며 방법을 추천해 달라는 응답이 자연스러움. 그림 개수는 이미 답한 내용이고, 벼룩시장은 다음 달에 열림.

passage: W: Kevin is the leader of his school's debate club. The club is holding a debate competition for first-year students next month. Kevin has prepared most of the event, including the topics and the schedule. However, he still needs two judges who can score the debates fairly and explain their decisions. He thinks Ms. Wilson, a social studies teacher, would be perfect for the role, because she often leads class discussions and gives students thoughtful feedback. Kevin knows she is very busy, but the competition only takes two hours on a Friday afternoon. So he decides to visit her office and ask if she could serve as a judge for the competition. In this situation, what would Kevin most likely say to Ms. Wilson?
question: 다음 상황 설명을 듣고, Kevin이 Ms. Wilson에게 할 말로 가장 적절한 것을 고르시오.
choices: Could you give me feedback on my social studies essay?
I'm sorry, but the competition has been canceled.
Would you be willing to judge our debate competition?
Why don't you join our debate club as a member?
explain_ko: 토론 대회 심사위원을 맡아 달라고 부탁하려는 상황. 에세이 피드백이나 동아리 가입 권유는 목적과 다름.

passage: M: Good morning, class. Have you ever signed up for a free trial of a music app or a video service? Companies give away their products for free, but they aren't just being generous. Today, let's look at why free trials work so well for businesses. First, once people start using a product, they begin to feel that it belongs to them, and giving it up feels like a loss. Second, a month is long enough to form a habit. After using an app every day, many people find it hard to live without it. Third, most free trials ask for card information at the start and then renew automatically. Many users simply forget to cancel before the first payment. Finally, even people who cancel have learned the product's name, which may bring them back later. Keep these points in mind before you click the free trial button.
question: 다음을 듣고, 남자가 하는 말의 주제로 가장 적절한 것을 고르시오.
choices: reasons why companies offer free trials to customers
how to cancel a subscription service easily
the history of music streaming services
explain_ko: 소유감, 습관 형성, 자동 결제, 이름 기억 효과 등 기업이 무료 체험을 주는 이유가 주제. 해지를 잊는 것은 이유 가운데 하나일 뿐 해지 방법을 설명하지는 않음.

passage: W: Hello, everyone. Today, we're going to talk about what people wrote on before paper became common. In ancient Mesopotamia, people pressed marks into soft clay with a sharp stick. When the clay dried, the writing became permanent, which is why many of these tablets survive today. In ancient Egypt, people made sheets from papyrus, a plant that grew along the Nile River. These sheets were light and easy to carry, but they fell apart in wet weather. In ancient China, people wrote on thin strips of bamboo that were tied together with string. However, these books were very heavy. In Europe, animal skin was used for important documents because it lasted a long time, although it was expensive to make. Now, let's see how paper changed all of this.
question: 다음을 듣고, 여자가 언급한 필기 재료가 아닌 것을 고르시오.
explain_ko: 점토, 파피루스, 대나무, 동물 가죽은 언급되었지만 돌은 나오지 않음.

passage: M: Rachel and her friend Sam have just arrived at the airport in a foreign city. It's six in the evening, and they need to get to their hotel downtown. Sam is tired after the long flight and suggests taking a taxi. However, Rachel checks her phone and finds that the roads to the city center are extremely crowded at this hour. According to the map, a taxi would take over an hour and cost about sixty dollars. On the other hand, the airport express train leaves every fifteen minutes, reaches downtown in thirty minutes, and costs only ten dollars per person. The hotel is also just a short walk from the train station. So Rachel wants to suggest that they take the train instead. In this situation, what would Rachel most likely say to Sam?
question: 다음 상황 설명을 듣고, Rachel이 Sam에게 할 말로 가장 적절한 것을 고르시오.
choices: We'd better arrive at the airport two hours early.
Why don't we take the train? It'll be faster and cheaper.
Let's take a taxi. The station is too far from the hotel.
How about walking to the hotel from the airport?
explain_ko: 택시는 막히고 비싸니 더 빠르고 싼 공항철도를 타자고 제안하려는 상황. 호텔은 역에서 가깝다고 했으므로 택시를 권하는 말은 반대.

question:
다음 영어 낱말의 뜻으로 알맞은 것은?
abstruse
explain_ko: abstruse는 이해하기 어렵고 '난해한'이라는 뜻이다.

question:
다음 빈칸에 알맞은 것은?
She felt _____ about the promotion, excited about the challenge but anxious about the added stress.
explain_ko: 기쁨과 불안이 동시에 있다는 문맥이므로 '양가적인, 이중적인 감정의'라는 뜻의 ambivalent가 알맞다.

question:
다음 영어 풀이에 해당하는 낱말은?
something that is different from what is normal or expected
explain_ko: 정상에서 벗어난 것을 뜻하는 anomaly에 대한 풀이이다.

question:
다음 문장에서 [apathy] 와 뜻이 가장 반대되는 것은?
Voter apathy has become a serious problem in recent local elections.
explain_ko: apathy는 '무관심'이라는 뜻이므로 반대말은 '열정'을 뜻하는 enthusiasm이다.

question:
다음 빈칸에 알맞은 것은?
The monastery's _____ lifestyle allowed for no luxury of any kind, only the bare essentials.
explain_ko: 사치가 전혀 없다는 문맥이므로 '검소한, 금욕적인'이라는 뜻의 austere가 알맞다.

question:
다음 영어 풀이에 해당하는 낱말은?
to give a false idea of something, or to show that something is not true
explain_ko: 겉보기와 실제가 다름을 보여준다는 뜻의 belie에 대한 풀이이다.

question:
다음 문장에서 [benevolent] 와 뜻이 가장 반대되는 것은?
The benevolent king was loved by all his people for his kindness.
explain_ko: benevolent는 '자비로운'이라는 뜻이므로 반대말은 '악의적인'을 뜻하는 malevolent이다.

question:
다음 영어 낱말의 뜻으로 알맞은 것은?
castigate
explain_ko: castigate는 잘못을 '심하게 비판하다, 질책하다'라는 뜻이다.

question:
다음 영어 풀이에 해당하는 낱말은?
careful to consider all possibilities and avoid risks
explain_ko: 위험을 피하려 신중히 살핀다는 뜻의 circumspect에 대한 풀이이다.

question:
다음 문장에서 [cogent] 와 뜻이 가장 비슷한 것은?
The lawyer presented a cogent argument that convinced the entire jury.
explain_ko: cogent는 '설득력 있는'이라는 뜻이므로 convincing과 가장 가깝다.

question:
다음 영어 낱말의 뜻으로 알맞은 것은?
complacent
explain_ko: complacent는 현재 상태에 '만족하여 안주하는'이라는 뜻이다.

question:
다음 빈칸에 알맞은 것은?
The school policy clearly states that it will not _____ any form of bullying among students.
explain_ko: 괴롭힘을 '눈감아주다, 묵과하다'라는 뜻의 condone이 문맥상 알맞다(묵과하지 않겠다는 의미).

question:
다음 문장에서 [convoluted] 와 뜻이 가장 비슷한 것은?
The instructions were so convoluted that nobody could assemble the shelf correctly.
explain_ko: convoluted는 '복잡하게 뒤얽힌'이라는 뜻이므로 complicated와 가장 가깝다.

question:
다음 영어 낱말의 뜻으로 알맞은 것은?
credulous
explain_ko: credulous는 남의 말을 '쉽게 믿는, 잘 속는'이라는 뜻이다.

question:
다음 빈칸에 알맞은 것은?
The long illness began to _____ his body, leaving him too weak to walk without help.
explain_ko: 몸을 약하게 만든다는 문맥이므로 '쇠약하게 하다'라는 뜻의 debilitate가 알맞다.

question:
다음 영어 풀이에 해당하는 낱말은?
to describe or explain something in a clear and detailed way
explain_ko: 무언가를 명확하고 상세하게 설명한다는 뜻의 delineate에 대한 풀이이다.

question:
다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 알맞은 것은?
_____ the Earth closer to the Sun, life as we know it could not exist.
explain_ko: If the Earth were closer 에서 If 를 생략하고 were 를 주어 앞으로 낸 가정법 과거 도치. Did, Had 는 뒤에 동사가 없고, If 만 쓰면 동사가 빠진다.

question: 다음 중 어법상 틀린 문장은?
choices: Had it not been for his advice, I would have failed.
Had I know about the sale, I would have bought the jacket.
Were I in your position, I would accept the offer.
Should you need any help, please call the front desk.
explain_ko: 가정법 과거완료 도치는 Had + 주어 + p.p. 이므로 Had I known 이 맞다. Were I, Should you, Had it not been for 는 바른 도치.

question:
두 문장의 뜻이 같도록 할 때 빈칸에 알맞은 것은?
If she had left home ten minutes earlier, she would not have missed the train.
= _____ home ten minutes earlier, she would not have missed the train.
explain_ko: If 를 생략하면 had 가 주어 앞으로 나와 Had she left. She had left 는 도치가 안 돼 조건절이 되지 못하고, Did/Were 는 시제·태가 맞지 않는다.

question:
다음 우리말을 영어로 바르게 옮긴 것은?
그의 도움이 없었더라면, 우리는 그 프로젝트를 끝내지 못했을 것이다.
choices: It had not been for his help, we could not have finished the project.
Had not it been for his help, we could not have finished the project.
Had it been not for his help, we could not have finished the project.
Had it not been for his help, we could not have finished the project.
explain_ko: If it had not been for 의 도치는 Had it not been for. not 은 주어 뒤에 오고, 도치하지 않은 It had not been 은 조건절이 되지 못한다.

question:
다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 알맞은 것은?
Only after the test results came out _____ how serious the problem was.
explain_ko: Only + 부사절이 문장 앞에 오면 주절이 도치되어 조동사 did + 주어 + 동사원형. we realized 는 도치가 안 된 오답.

question: 다음 중 어법상 틀린 문장은?
choices: On the top of the hill stands an old stone tower.
Not until last year he did start learning to swim.
Little did she know that her friends were planning a party.
It was in the library that I first met my best friend.
explain_ko: Not until 이 앞에 오면 did he start 로 도치해야 한다. it ~ that 강조, 장소 부사구 도치, Little did 도치는 바르다.

question:
두 문장의 뜻이 같도록 할 때 빈칸에 알맞은 것은?
He did not understand the value of health until he became ill.
= It was not until he became ill _____ he understood the value of health.
explain_ko: '~하고 나서야 비로소 …했다'는 It was not until ~ that … 강조 구문. when/which/what 은 이 구문에 쓰지 않는다.

question:
다음 우리말을 영어로 바르게 옮긴 것은?
우리가 그 문제를 해결한 것은 바로 수학 동아리의 도움 덕분이었다.
choices: It was thanks to the math club's help that we solved the problem.
That was thanks to the math club's help it we solved the problem.
It thanks to the math club's help was that we solved the problem.
It was that thanks to the math club's help we solved the problem.
explain_ko: 강조할 부사구를 It was 와 that 사이에 두는 it ~ that 강조 구문. that 이 강조 대상 앞에 오거나 was 가 뒤로 밀리면 틀린다.

question:
다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 알맞은 것은?
The claim that plants, which cannot move, are unable to respond to their surroundings _____ now considered false by most biologists.
explain_ko: 주어는 The claim(단수)이고 that ~ surroundings 는 동격절, which cannot move 는 삽입이다. 본동사가 필요하므로 is. are 는 가까운 plants 에 끌린 오답.

question: 다음 중 어법상 틀린 문장은?
choices: Though tired after the long journey, the travelers kept walking toward the village.
The rumor that the factory would close were spread quickly across the town.
The belief that hard work always pays off, however popular, is not always true.
The scientist, it seems, had overlooked a small but important detail.
explain_ko: 동격절을 빼면 주어는 The rumor(단수)이므로 was spread 가 맞다. it seems 삽입, Though tired 생략, however popular 삽입은 바르다.

question:
두 문장의 뜻이 같도록 할 때 빈칸에 알맞은 것은?
If it is used properly, this tool can save you a lot of time.
= If _____, this tool can save you a lot of time.
explain_ko: 부사절의 '주어+be동사(it is)'를 생략하면 If used properly. 도구는 '사용되는' 대상이므로 using 은 태가 틀리고, it used 는 be동사만 빠진 오류.

question:
다음 우리말을 영어로 바르게 옮긴 것은?
그 계획이 실패할 것이라는 그의 예측은, 놀랍게도, 옳았다.
choices: His prediction was that the plan would fail, surprisingly, correct.
That his prediction the plan would fail was, surprisingly, correct.
His prediction that the plan would fail was, surprisingly, correct.
His prediction, surprisingly, that the plan would fail correct was.
explain_ko: 동격절 that the plan would fail 이 주어 His prediction 바로 뒤에 붙고, 삽입어 surprisingly 는 동사 was 와 보어 correct 사이에 들어간다.

question:
다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 알맞은 것은?
Anyone who has tried to learn a new language knows how difficult it is to keep _____ after the first few months.
explain_ko: keep 뒤 보어 자리이고 주어가 '동기를 부여받는' 입장이므로 과거분사 motivated. motivating 은 목적어가 있어야 하는 능동, motivate/to motivate 는 keep 의 보어가 될 수 없다.

question: 다음 중 어법상 틀린 문장은?
choices: The questions she asked were so difficult that few students could answer them.
Hardly had the concert begun when the lights were gone out.
What matters is not how fast you read but how much you understand.
Not only does exercise strengthen the body, but it also improves mood.
explain_ko: go out(꺼지다)은 자동사라 수동태로 쓸 수 없으므로 went out 이 맞다. 나머지는 so ~ that, what 주어절, Not only 도치가 모두 바르다.

question:
두 문장의 뜻이 같도록 할 때 빈칸에 알맞은 것은?
It seems that the ancient tribe used the cave as a shelter.
= The ancient tribe seems _____ the cave as a shelter.
explain_ko: seems(현재)보다 used(과거)가 앞선 시점이므로 완료부정사 to have used. to use 는 시제가, to have been used 는 태가 틀리다.

question:
다음 우리말을 영어로 바르게 옮긴 것은?
그가 한 말이 사실인지는 아무도 확신할 수 없었다.
choices: Nobody could be sure what whether he said was true.
Nobody could be sure what he said whether was true.
Nobody could be sure whether was what he said true.
Nobody could be sure whether what he said was true.
explain_ko: whether 절 안에서 주어 what he said 다음에 동사 was 가 온다. what 과 whether 의 순서를 바꾸거나 was 를 주어 앞에 두면 틀린다.

passage:
Dear Councilmember Alvarez,
I am writing as a resident of the Eastside neighborhood who has lived three blocks from the Orion Theater for more than thirty years. I recently read in the local newspaper that the city is considering a proposal to demolish the building next spring and replace it with a parking structure. I fully understand that the theater has been closed for several years and that parking in the area is limited. Nevertheless, I believe that tearing down the Orion would be a serious mistake. Built in 1928, it is one of the last remaining examples of its architectural style in our region, and its painted ceiling and original stage are still in remarkably good condition. Similar buildings in other cities have been restored as community arts centers and have brought new visitors and businesses to their neighborhoods. Before any final decision is made, I respectfully ask that the council delay the vote and hold a public hearing so that residents and preservation experts can present alternative plans for the building. I would be glad to help organize such a meeting.
Respectfully yours,
Margaret Olsen
question: 다음 글의 목적으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 극장을 예술 센터로 바꾸는 공사에 자원봉사자로 지원하려고
신문에 실린 극장 관련 기사의 오류 정정을 요구하려고
극장 건물 철거 결정을 미루고 공청회를 열어 줄 것을 요청하려고
극장 주변의 주차 공간 부족 문제 해결을 건의하려고
explain_ko: 'ask that the council delay the vote and hold a public hearing'이 핵심. 주차 부족은 필자가 인정하는 상대 논리일 뿐이고, 도우겠다는 것도 공사가 아니라 회의 준비다.

passage: Marcus slammed the car door and stared at the steam rising from under the hood. The rental car had broken down on a narrow country road, twenty kilometers from the nearest town, and the rain that had been threatening all afternoon was now falling steadily. He had an important meeting with a client in two hours, and he had chosen this shortcut precisely to save time. Muttering about the rental company and the terrible road, he kicked a loose stone into the ditch and tried calling for help, only to hear a recorded message telling him that all operators were busy. Just then, an old pickup truck came around the bend and slowed to a stop beside him. A gray-haired woman leaned out of the window, asked what had happened, and without a moment's hesitation offered to tow the car to her nephew's garage in the village. While the mechanic worked, she served Marcus hot tea in her kitchen and even lent him her phone to reschedule the meeting. When the car was finally ready, he pressed her hand warmly, searching for words that could express how much her kindness had meant to him.

passage: Helene Marsh, a photographer whose images of polar landscapes are now displayed in museums around the world, was born in 1932 in Scotland. She received her first camera at the age of twelve from an uncle who worked as a ship's engineer, and she spent her teenage years photographing the fishing boats in her hometown harbor. Although she was accepted to study chemistry at university, she left after two years to work as an assistant in a portrait studio in London, where she learned to develop film and control light. In 1961, she joined a scientific expedition to Greenland as its official photographer, becoming one of the first women to take on such a role. The harsh conditions often froze her equipment, so she designed a special insulated case that other expedition photographers later adopted. Her 1968 book, which combined her photographs with the diary she kept during the journey, became a bestseller and inspired a generation of nature photographers. She spent her final years teaching free photography workshops for young people in rural communities and died in 2011 at the age of seventy-nine.

passage: In many suburbs, a smooth green lawn is regarded as the mark of a well-kept home. Maintaining one, however, comes at a surprisingly high cost. Lawns in dry regions can consume a large share of a household's water during summer, and keeping the grass uniform often requires regular applications of fertilizers and weed killers that wash into nearby streams. Frequent mowing adds noise and fuel use. Moreover, for all this effort, a lawn offers very little to wildlife: a short carpet of a single type of grass provides almost no food or shelter for insects, and without insects, the birds that depend on them to feed their young also disappear. Plants that naturally grow in the region are a far better choice. Because they are adapted to the local rainfall and soil, they need little extra water or chemicals once established, and they support the native insects that have evolved alongside them over thousands of years. Homeowners and local governments should therefore replace at least part of their lawns with native plants, turning spaces that only consume resources into small habitats that give something back to the ecosystem around them.

passage: We usually assume that the more someone knows about a field, the better that person will be at solving its problems. In most situations this is true, but deep expertise carries a hidden cost. Over years of training, experts develop efficient mental shortcuts: they quickly recognize familiar patterns and apply solutions that have worked before. These shortcuts save enormous time when a problem resembles past cases, yet they can also narrow what the expert is able to notice. When a problem requires an unusual approach, the expert's mind tends to slide back toward the familiar answer, while alternative possibilities are dismissed before they are seriously considered. Studies of skilled chess players, for instance, have found that once they spot a well-known winning plan, they often fail to see a shorter and better one on the same board, even when told to look for it. Newcomers, lacking such habits, sometimes stumble upon solutions precisely because they do not know what is supposed to be impossible. This is why innovative organizations often mix experienced members with outsiders who can ask naive questions.

passage: Anthropologists have long been puzzled by rituals that seem to serve no practical purpose. Across cultures, people march in synchronized steps, sing the same songs at the same moment, or perform elaborate ceremonies that require weeks of preparation and considerable expense. From a purely economic point of view, this time and energy could be used for more productive activities. Yet rituals appear in every known human society, which suggests that they meet some deep need. One widely supported explanation is that rituals strengthen the bonds among group members. Laboratory studies have found that people who move or sing in unison with others afterward report feeling closer to them and are more willing to cooperate in games that require trust. Rituals that involve shared hardship, such as long fasts or difficult journeys, seem to produce especially strong loyalty, perhaps because participants come to see one another as people who have proved their commitment. By turning individuals into a group that feels and acts as one, rituals help communities face challenges that no single person could overcome alone.

passage: For much of the last century, forest managers treated dead trees as a problem to be removed. Standing dead trunks looked untidy, seemed to invite disease, and were considered a waste of wood that could have been sold. Ecologists now see them very differently. A dead tree may remain standing for decades, and during that time it becomes one of the busiest places in the forest. Woodpeckers carve nesting holes in its softening wood, and when they move on, owls, bats, and squirrels take over the empty spaces. Beetles and fungi slowly break down the trunk, providing food for birds and returning nutrients to the soil. Even after it falls, the log continues to serve as shelter for salamanders and as a moist bed in which new seedlings can take root. Researchers estimate that a large share of forest species, from tiny insects to large birds, depend on dead wood at some stage of their lives. As a result, many forest agencies now deliberately leave a certain number of dead trees standing, recognizing that a forest without them is poorer, not cleaner.

passage: Many people imagine that the work of a historian is simply to collect facts about the past and arrange them in the correct order. In reality, historical sources rarely speak for themselves, and the historian must decide how to read them. ① A letter written by a government official, for example, may reveal as much about what the writer wanted his superiors to believe as about what actually happened. ② Handwriting in the nineteenth century was often taught through strict daily exercises, and many schools awarded prizes for the most elegant script. ③ Similarly, the absence of certain groups from official records, such as women, servants, or the poor, does not mean that they played no role in events, only that those who kept the records did not consider them worth mentioning. ④ For this reason, historians compare many kinds of evidence, ask who produced each document and for what purpose, and remain aware that their own questions are shaped by the concerns of the present. History, in this sense, is less a finished record than an ongoing conversation between the past and those who study it.

Until the middle of the twentieth century, loading a cargo ship was slow and exhausting work. Goods arrived at the port in sacks, barrels, and wooden crates of every size, and teams of dockworkers carried them on board one piece at a time.

(A) The solution turned out to be simple: a steel box of standard size that could be packed at the factory, sealed, and moved from truck to train to ship without ever being opened. Because every box had the same dimensions, cranes could lift one in minutes, and ships could be designed to stack them like building blocks.

(B) As a result, a ship often spent more time sitting in port than sailing across the ocean, and handling cargo could make up a large part of the total cost of shipping. Theft and damage were also common, since each item passed through many hands.

(C) The effects of this change reached far beyond the docks. Shipping costs fell so sharply that it became profitable to make parts in one country, assemble them in another, and sell the products worldwide. At the same time, old port districts lost thousands of jobs as automated terminals were built outside the city centers.

passage: When a plant or animal is carried to a new continent, it usually fails to survive, because the local climate, soil, or food supply does not suit it. Occasionally, however, a newcomer not only survives but spreads so rapidly that it pushes native species aside. ( ① ) Ecologists have proposed several explanations for such success, and one of the most widely supported concerns the enemies the species left behind. ( ② ) In its original home, every species is kept in check by a set of insects, diseases, and predators that have evolved alongside it over thousands of years. ( ③ ) When the species is moved to a distant region, it often arrives without these companions, while the native plants and animals around it remain under full attack from their own enemies. ( ④ ) This is why some control programs deliberately introduce a carefully tested insect from the invader's homeland, hoping to restore the balance that the invader escaped. Such programs require years of testing, however, since the introduced insect could itself become a new problem.

passage: Long before electric heating and air conditioning, builders in different parts of the world developed clever ways to keep homes comfortable using only local materials and careful design. ① Modern apartment buildings in large cities are often sold at high prices because of the wide views that their glass walls offer. ② In hot, dry regions, houses were constructed with thick walls of mud or stone that absorbed the heat of the day slowly and released it during the cold desert night. ③ Many traditional buildings in these areas also featured narrow streets and inner courtyards, which created shade and allowed cooler air to settle near the ground. ④ In humid tropical climates, by contrast, homes were raised on posts and given steep roofs and open walls, so that breezes could pass through the rooms and heavy rain could run off quickly. Today, architects are looking for ways to reduce the energy consumed by buildings. passage: Endurance athletes are famous for their discipline. They run, swim, or cycle for hours each day, and many of them feel guilty whenever they miss a single session. It may therefore surprise people to learn that in the final one or two weeks before a major race, most coaches ask their athletes to train far less than usual. This practice, known as tapering, is based on a simple fact about the body: training itself does not make an athlete stronger. Hard workouts cause tiny damage to muscles and drain the body's energy stores, and it is during the recovery that follows that the body rebuilds itself to be more capable than before. When athletes keep training hard right up to the competition, they arrive at the starting line tired, with the benefits of months of work still hidden beneath their fatigue. Reducing the load allows those benefits to finally appear. For many athletes, the hardest part of this stage is psychological, because they must trust that [doing less is also doing the work]. Those who cannot resist one last difficult workout often discover that they have spent their best performance in practice.

passage: Anyone who studies vocabulary closely soon notices a curious pattern: the words people use most often tend to be short. In English, words such as the, of, and, and is are among the most common, and nearly all of them have a single syllable, while rare words like photosynthesis or bureaucracy stretch across several. This is not a coincidence. When a long word begins to be used frequently, speakers gradually trim it to save effort. Omnibus became bus, telephone became phone, and television is now often simply TV. Nobody decides on these changes; they spread because shorter forms are quicker to say, and listeners can still understand them from context. Frequency protects words in another way as well. Irregular verbs such as go and went have survived for centuries, while many less common irregular verbs have gradually become regular, because rarely used forms are more easily forgotten and replaced by the general rule. Language, then, is shaped by the everyday habits of its speakers, and one of its steadiest tendencies is that the more often a word is used, _____.

passage: History is full of inventions that were technically superior to their rivals and yet failed to catch on. A common explanation is poor marketing, but a closer look suggests a deeper cause. New technologies do not enter an empty world; they enter a world already organized around existing tools, skills, and routines. An invention that requires people to abandon these arrangements all at once asks them to pay a high price in time, effort, and uncertainty, even if it promises long-term benefits. By contrast, an invention that can be adopted gradually, alongside familiar practices, lowers that price considerably. Early automobiles, for example, were often described as horseless carriages and were designed to resemble the vehicles people already knew, while some of the first electric lighting companies deliberately made their bulbs similar in brightness to the gas lamps they were replacing. In both cases, the new technology spread not because it demanded a revolution in daily life but because it _____. Inventors who ignore this lesson may build remarkable machines that end up only in museums.

passage: Many companies now use computer programs to screen job applications, hoping to make the process faster and fairer. These programs learn by studying records of past hiring decisions: they identify the features shared by applicants who were hired and then look for similar features in new applications. The idea sounds objective, since a machine has no personal likes or dislikes. The difficulty is that past decisions were made by people, and people's judgments were not always fair. If a company had mostly hired graduates of a few universities, or had rarely given technical positions to women, the program would treat these patterns as signs of a good employee. It might then give lower scores to applicants who mentioned a women's sports club or a less well-known school, without anyone having told it to do so. Worse, because the program's calculations are complex and hidden, such unfairness can be harder to notice and challenge than the biased opinion of a single manager. For this reason, some experts argue that automated systems should be tested regularly with sample applications to reveal whose chances they are quietly reducing.

passage:

question: 대화를 듣고, Reading Buddies에 관해 언급되지 않은 것을 고르시오.
explain_ko: 대상(초등 1·2학년), 활동 요일(화·목)과 기간, 수료증과 봉사 20시간, 하루 사전 교육은 나오지만 모집 인원은 나오지 않음.

passage: M: Attention, visitors. Welcome to the Silver Lake Wetland Center. We're pleased to introduce our special bird-watching tour, which runs every weekend this autumn. The tour begins at seven in the morning, when the birds are most active, and lasts about two hours. An experienced guide will lead groups of no more than ten people along a quiet path through the reeds. Binoculars will be provided free of charge, but please bring your own water. Children under ten must be accompanied by an adult. Because the birds are easily frightened, we ask that you talk quietly and avoid wearing bright clothes. Tickets can be booked only at the information desk.
question: 다음을 듣고, 철새 관찰 투어에 관한 내용과 일치하지 않는 것을 고르시오.
choices: 입장권은 안내 데스크에서만 예약할 수 있다.

오전 7시에 시작하여 약 두 시간 동안 진행된다.
explain_ko: 쌍안경은 무료로 제공(free of charge)되므로 불일치. 시작 시각·소요 시간, 그룹 인원, 안내 데스크 예약은 모두 일치.

passage: W: Good afternoon, listeners. I'm Linda Brooks, the director of the Oakwood History Museum. Next spring, our museum will celebrate the two hundredth anniversary of our town with a special exhibition called Oakwood Through the Years. We want this exhibition to show not just famous events, but the everyday lives of ordinary people who lived here. That's where we need your help. Many of you may have old photographs, letters, school uniforms, or kitchen tools stored in your attics and basements. These items may seem unimportant to you, but they can tell powerful stories about our town's past. If you have anything you'd be willing to donate or lend to the museum, please contact us by the end of January. Our staff will visit your home to look at the items. Together, we can build an exhibition that truly belongs to everyone.
question: 다음을 듣고, 여자가 하는 말의 목적으로 가장 적절한 것을 고르시오.
choices: 다락방과 지하실의 물건 정리 방법을 안내하려고

explain_ko: 마을 200주년 전시회를 위해 집에 있는 옛 사진·편지·교복 등을 기증하거나 빌려 달라는 요청이 목적. 200주년은 박물관이 아니라 마을의 것이라 두 번째 선택지는 함정.

passage:
W: Dad, I finished my report on climate change already. It only took me thirty minutes.
M: Thirty minutes? That's fast. How did you do it?
W: I asked an AI chatbot, and it wrote most of the report for me.
M: Hmm. Did you check whether the information is accurate?
W: Not really. It sounded very confident, so I assumed it was correct.
M: That's the risky part. AI tools sometimes give wrong facts or even make up sources that don't exist.
W: Really? I didn't know that.
M: They can be useful for getting ideas, but you should always check the facts with reliable sources, like government reports or academic articles.
W: That sounds like a lot of extra work.
M: It is, but if you hand in wrong information, your teacher will notice. More importantly, you won't actually learn anything.
W: I see your point. I'll go through the report and check each fact.
question: 대화를 듣고, 남자의 의견으로 가장 적절한 것을 고르시오.
choices: 보고서를 쓸 때 인공지능 도구를 사용해서는 안 된다.
인공지능이 준 정보는 믿을 만한 자료로 사실 여부를 확인해야 한다.
기후 변화 보고서에는 정부 자료를 반드시 인용해야 한다.
과제는 충분한 시간을 들여 천천히 해야 한다.
explain_ko: 남자는 AI가 틀린 사실이나 가짜 출처를 낼 수 있으니 믿을 만한 자료로 확인하라고 함. AI가 아이디어를 얻는 데는 유용하다고 했으므로 쓰지 말라는 것은 아님.

passage: M: Hello, parents. I'm Dr. Paul Bennett, a child psychologist. Today, I want to talk about how you praise your children. When a child gets a good grade, many parents say, you're so smart. It sounds like a kind thing to say, but it can actually have a negative effect. Children who are praised for being smart often start to believe that ability is fixed. As a result, they may avoid difficult tasks, because they're afraid that failing will prove they're not smart after all. Instead, try praising their effort and the process. Say something like, you worked really hard on this, or I like the way you tried different methods. This kind of praise teaches children that they can improve through effort, and it helps them face challenges with confidence.
question: 다음을 듣고, 남자가 하는 말의 요지로 가장 적절한 것을 고르시오.
choices: 칭찬을 자주 하면 아이가 칭찬에 의존하게 된다.
아이의 성적이 오르면 바로 보상해 주는 것이 좋다.
아이를 칭찬할 때는 타고난 능력보다 노력과 과정을 칭찬해야 한다.
아이가 어려운 과제를 피하게 해야 자신감이 생긴다.
explain_ko: '똑똑하다'는 능력 칭찬 대신 노력과 과정을 칭찬해야 아이가 도전에 자신감을 갖는다는 것이 요지. 칭찬 자체를 줄이라는 말은 없음.

passage:

W: It's about an hour by subway, but I wouldn't have minded that.

M: That makes sense. I'm sure you made the right choice.

question: 대화를 듣고, 여자의 마지막 말에 대한 남자의 응답으로 가장 적절한 것을 고르시오.

passage:

passage: W: Andrew recently started an internship at a marketing company. His manager, Ms. Parker, asked him to write a report analyzing last month's sales. However, she knows that the company's directors are extremely busy and usually spend only a few minutes on each report. She worries that they may not find the most important findings buried among so many pages. So she wants Andrew to keep his detailed analysis but add a short summary of the key points at the very beginning of the report. In this situation, what would Ms. Parker most likely say to Andrew?
question: 다음 상황 설명을 듣고, Ms. Parker가 Andrew에게 할 말로 가장 적절한 것을 고르시오.
choices: You should collect more data to support your analysis.

passage: M: Good afternoon, class. When we think of inventions that changed the world, we usually picture computers or airplanes. But today, I'd like to talk about something much simpler: the steel shipping container. Before containers became common, goods were loaded onto ships one bag or box at a time. This process required huge numbers of workers and could take several days for a single ship. Goods were also often damaged or stolen at the port. Standard containers changed all of this. Because they're all the same size, giant cranes can move them directly from ships to trucks and trains. Loading time dropped from days to hours, and shipping costs fell sharply. As a result, companies could make goods in one country and sell them cheaply on the other side of the world. In short, this simple metal box helped make modern global trade possible.
question: 다음을 듣고, 남자가 하는 말의 주제로 가장 적절한 것을 고르시오.
choices: the development of faster cargo ships and trains
how the shipping container transformed global trade
ways to prevent goods from being stolen at ports
why port workers lost their jobs to cranes
explain_ko: 규격화된 컨테이너가 하역 시간과 운송비를 줄여 세계 무역을 가능하게 했다는 것이 주제. 도난·크레인은 설명 과정의 세부 내용.

passage: W: Hello, everyone. Today, we're going to look at how cities are fighting extreme summer heat. Cities are often several degrees hotter than the surrounding countryside, because concrete and asphalt absorb heat during the day and release it at night. Fortunately, there are several effective solutions. First, many cities are building green roofs, which are covered with plants that cool the air and keep buildings cooler inside. Second, some cities are painting roofs and roads with special white paint that reflects sunlight instead of absorbing it. Third, planting trees along streets provides shade and lowers the temperature of the ground below. Some cities have also installed systems that spray a fine mist of water in crowded public spaces. These methods can reduce city temperatures and save lives during heat waves. Now, let's look at one city that has combined all of these ideas.
question: 다음을 듣고, 여자가 도시의 더위를 줄이는 방법으로 언급하지 않은 것을 고르시오.
explain_ko: 옥상 녹화, 햇빛을 반사하는 흰 페인트, 가로수, 물안개 분사 장치는 나오지만 그늘막 버스 정류장은 나오지 않음.

passage: M: Sophia and Ethan are hiking up a mountain they have wanted to climb for a long time. They left early in the morning and are now about an hour away from the top. Ethan is excited and wants to keep going, since they have come so far. However, Sophia notices that dark clouds are quickly gathering over the peak, and the wind is getting stronger. She checks the weather app on her phone and sees a warning that a thunderstorm is expected within the next hour. She knows that being on an open mountaintop during a thunderstorm can be extremely dangerous. Although she is also disappointed, she believes their safety is more important than reaching the summit, and they can always try again another day. In this situation, what would Sophia most likely say to Ethan?
question: 다음 상황 설명을 듣고, Sophia가 Ethan에게 할 말로 가장 적절한 것을 고르시오.
choices: Could you take a picture of me at the summit?
I think we should have brought more snacks with us.
Let's hurry up so we can reach the top before the storm.
We should head back down. The summit will still be here next time.
explain_ko: 천둥번개가 곧 올 것이라 안전을 위해 내려가고 다음에 다시 오자고 하려는 상황. 폭풍 전에 서둘러 정상에 가자는 말은 Ethan의 생각에 가까움.
